ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all general partners, directors, authorized signatories, and every individual owning or controlling 25% or more against: FINTRAC politically exposed persons and heads of international organizations criteria; Canadian targeted sanctions lists maintained under the Special Economic Measures Act, United Nations Act, and Criminal Code; OFAC SDN list for USD clearing and correspondent banking; and adverse media, enforcement, and regulatory action databases. Evidence of screening must be retained for at least five years after termination of the business relationship.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: The legal name of a British Columbia limited partnership must be in English or French letters using the standard Roman alphabet. Non-Latin scripts are not accepted in the registered legal name; a transliterated and translated name must be supplied. The name must include the legal element 'Limited Partnership' or an accepted abbreviation such as 'L.P.'. Descriptive terms such as 'UHT Oat Milk' must not be misleading, and use of dairy-derived terms may require confirmation under federal CFIA labelling rules before registration.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: If a BC name reservation is rejected, the applicant should review the registrar's stated reason, correct the conflicting or prohibited element, and file a new name request. A written reconsideration may be submitted to the BC Registrar of Companies with the original name request number and supporting consent letters or submissions. If the rejection is confirmed, the applicant may seek judicial review before the Supreme Court of British Columbia under the Judicial Review Procedure Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 241. Any extension of an existing reservation must be requested before expiry; otherwise a new reservation must be filed.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A virtual office is permitted solely as a BC registered office if it is a physical street address in British Columbia attended during normal business hours for service of process; a post office box is not sufficient. A virtual office cannot satisfy commercial substance requirements for the UHT oat milk facility, which must have an actual production plant licensed under the Safe Food for Canadians Regulations and applicable BC food safety requirements.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: High; pre-operational CFIA inspection is mandatory and virtually certain at 100%, and the probability of at least one unannounced physical on-site inspection during the first 12 months of UHT plant operation is estimated at greater than 80%.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada — national competent authority for GST/HST, federal income tax, payroll, and entity tax accounts, with the primary digital portal being My Business Account (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency.html; https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/digital-services-businesses/business-account.html). For the British Columbia Provincial Sales Tax (PST), the competent authority is the BC Ministry of Finance, Consumer Taxation Branch, administered via the eTaxBC portal (https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/taxes/sales-taxes/PST/etaxbc). The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is the competent authority for customs export declarations, and the BC Registrar of Companies (BC Registry Online) administers the underlying statutory LP registration under the BC Limited Partnership Act, RSBC 1996, c. 341.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Register the BC limited partnership with the BC Registrar of Companies via BC Registry Online, filing the Limited Partnership Statement of Information and identifying each general partner and limited partner, including non-resident beneficial owners. Step 2: Establish the Canadian permanent establishment footprint and request the federal 9-digit Business Number (BN) from the CRA using Form RC1 or the Business Registration Online (BRO) service, activating the GST/HST account (RT code), payroll account (RP), and import/export program accounts (RM/RS) as applicable; an income tax account is not required for the partnership itself because the LP is fiscally transparent. Step 3: Register as a BC PST vendor through eTaxBC if the LP makes taxable retail sales in BC or has a place of business in BC; there is no small-supplier PST exemption. Step 4: If any equity interest is held by non-residents, the LP must file the T5013 Partnership Information Return annually, appoint a CRA representative (Form RC59), and ensure that the non-resident partners' Canadian-source allocation is documented under the partnership agreement. The CRA issues the BN and GST/HST registration immediately upon electronic filing; the effective GST/HST registration date is the earlier of the date the LP first makes a taxable supply in Canada and the date of registration, subject to the CAD 30,000 small-supplier threshold.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Pass_Through_Eligible — a British Columbia limited partnership is fiscally transparent for federal and provincial corporate income tax under the Income Tax Act; the partnership itself is not a taxpayer and each partner, including a non-resident limited partner, is taxed on its allocated share of Canadian-source income, gains, losses, and credits. For indirect tax, however, the Excise Tax Act deems the partnership to be a person and requires the LP to obtain its own BN and GST/HST registration, file separate GST/HST returns, and remit GST as the registered supplier. For BC PST, the LP is the vendor and collection agent for the 7% provincial retail sales tax. The LP may qualify as a Canadian partnership under ITA s. 102 only if every partner is resident in Canada; if one or more limited partners are non-resident, the LP is not a Canadian partnership but retains its pass-through status, subject to enhanced T5013 reporting and transfer-pricing documentation. The appropriate classification for this dossier is therefore Pass_Through_Eligible with a Canadian permanent establishment in British Columbia.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not have a US-style check-the-box entity classification election. The relevant statutory elections and mechanisms for this cross-border LP are: (1) ITA s. 216.1 election — the non-resident limited partners, through the partnership, may elect to file a full Part I net-basis Canadian income tax return rather than being subject to gross-basis Part XIII non-resident withholding on partnership distributions; (2) ITA s. 17.1 functional-currency election, subject to CRA approval, allowing the LP to compute Canadian tax results in US dollars where the plant keeps its books in USD; (3) ETA s. 156 election to allow the LP and an associated GST registrant to file one combined GST/HST return, which may be used if the oat milk plant operates under an integrated group; (4) US federal Form 8832 election by the US partner to treat the Canadian LP as a partnership or as an association taxable as a corporation for US federal tax purposes, which must be carefully reconciled against Canada's OECD hybrid mismatch rules in ITA ss. 12.3 and 18.4 to prevent inappropriate double-non-taxation or duplicate deduction outcomes; and (5) a BC PST manufacturing and production machinery exemption application, filed through eTaxBC, to exempt the aseptic UHT plant equipment and qualifying packaging-line machinery from the 7% PST.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (federal value-added tax) in British Columbia at 5%, operating alongside the British Columbia Provincial Sales Tax (PST) at 7%; the two taxes are separate levies — the GST is an invoice-credit VAT administered by the federal CRA, whereas the BC PST is a retail sales tax administered by the BC Ministry of Finance (Consumer Taxation Branch).
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: GST/HST: CAD 30,000 in cumulative taxable supplies made in Canada during the current calendar quarter or the preceding four calendar quarters, with mandatory registration effective before the earlier of the date taxable supplies are first made after losing small-supplier status and 30 days after the threshold is exceeded. BC PST: no small-supplier registration threshold exists; the LP must register as a BC PST vendor through eTaxBC if it maintains a place of business in BC or makes taxable retail sales in BC. Export sales delivered outside BC are exempt from PST, but the vendor registration obligation remains for any BC retail activity.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No mandatory real-time fiscal clearance, government invoice stamping, or continuous transaction control regime exists in Canada as of the current tax compliance pipeline. The CRA accepts electronic invoices and retained records where they are accurate, legible, and reproducible for the statutory six-year retention period; GST/HST returns are filed electronically through GST/HST NETFILE, My Business Account, or certified EDI, but invoices themselves are not transmitted to the CRA for clearance. The CBSA, however, operates the Canadian Export Reporting System (CERS), which requires electronic pre-export declaration data through a certified service provider API for all commercial export shipments exceeding CAD 2,000, generating an acknowledgement message that serves as the fiscal export clearance record. The Pan-Canadian Peppol-based e-Invoicing framework is voluntary for B2B and B2G transactions; the aseptic UHT oat milk plant should nevertheless design its ERP to archive CERS acknowledgements, batch-level production records, and electronic invoices in a machine-readable format to support future audits.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: GST: Under the Excise Tax Act, Schedule VI, Part I, a supply of goods by a registered supplier is zero-rated where the supplier exports the goods in the course of its commercial activity; the packaged UHT oat milk cartons sold to non-resident distributors qualify for 0% GST where the sale contract, Incoterms 2020 delivery term, freight engagement, and CBSA export documentation collectively establish that the goods left Canada as part of and in connection with the supply. Services, including tolling and co-packaging services performed at the plant for a non-resident principal, are zero-rated under Schedule VI, Part V when the benefit of the service is consumed outside Canada. Additionally, domestic supplies of basic groceries, a category that includes most unflavoured plant-based beverage formats such as oat milk sold as a food for human consumption, may already be zero-rated under Schedule VI, Part III, so the LP can claim full 5% input tax credits on raw materials, packaging inputs, and production overhead while remitting no GST on qualifying grocery-format cartons. BC PST: export sales are exempt from PST where the vendor delivers the goods to the buyer outside BC/Canada, and the UHT aseptic plant's production and packaging machinery is eligible for the BC PST manufacturing and production machinery exemption.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: CBSA Export Declaration (CERS / Form B13A or certified EDI-CSP transmission) for all consignments exceeding CAD 2,000
Original or electronic Bill of Lading, air waybill, or through rail/road waybill evidencing continuous carriage to the foreign destination
Inward Remittance Certificate / SWIFT MT103 or MT202 settlement confirmation matching the export invoice and the LP's foreign-currency bank ledger
Commercial invoice containing the zero-rated export statement and Incoterms 2020 delivery term
GST tax invoice or approved simplified supporting record showing the supplier's BN and the zero-rating basis
Packing list, container seal record, and aseptic UHT batch/lot traceability documentation reconciling production output to shipment
Copy of the foreign purchase order or supply contract identifying the non-resident purchaser and final destination country
Freight forwarder certificate of export and carrier terminal or foreign customs clearance notification
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: The CRA has a normal four-year reassessment window for GST/HST, extended indefinitely where a person has made a misrepresentation or committed fraud. If export zero-rating is disallowed, the LP will be assessed 5% GST on the export proceeds, lose the corresponding input tax credits, and owe compound daily interest from the original filing due date. Statutory penalties include the ETA s. 285 false-statement penalty equal to 25% of the understated net tax and the ITA s. 163(2) gross-negligence penalty equal to 50% of understated income where income tax is also understated; criminal prosecution under ITA s. 239 or ETA s. 327 for deliberate evasion may lead to fines of 50% to 200% of the tax evaded and imprisonment of up to two years per count. The CBSA can independently impose administrative monetary penalties of up to CAD 25,000 per violation for failure to file accurate export declarations or for late, incomplete, or non-compliant CERS transmissions. The LP must retain export books and records for six years under ETA s. 286, and the CRA may issue a requirement under ITA s. 231(1) to produce records held outside Canada. Particular audit scrutiny applies to related-party export sales, offshore tolling arrangements, and export invoices not matched by inbound SWIFT settlement; the general partner may be personally assessed if it directed, assented to, or acquiesced in improper zero-rating. Canada imposes no statutory 180-day foreign-exchange repatriation deadline; the 180-day parameter in this dossier is adopted as the group's treasury and transfer-pricing documentation benchmark for confirming that export receivables are actually settled and traceable.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains current account convertibility with capital account transactions subject to Bank of Canada oversight. Profit remittances to non-resident limited partners are permitted subject to Income Tax Act compliance, FINTRAC reporting, and provision of audited financial statements; no material regulatory hurdles exist for legitimate business distributions.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canadian exporters must repatriate export proceeds to Canada within six months under the Export and Import Act. No mandatory conversion ratio applies; proceeds are deposited into the exporter's Canadian dollar account.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low feasibility for offshore digital EMIs; Canadian regulations under FINTRAC and OSFI impose strict licensing and compliance requirements on cross-border electronic money issuance and transfer services.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Remote KYC and account opening is permitted for British Columbia Limited Partnerships; physical presence of directors or authorized signatories is not mandatory unless the relationship is classified as high-risk by the bank.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade disbursements facilitated through SWIFT MT103 for international payments and Commercial Letters of Credit for trade settlements. statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory audit requirement under BC Limited Partnership Act; audit triggers may arise from partnership agreement or if gross revenue exceeds CAD 10 million for GST/HST rebate claims. statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises) or IFRS if elective or required by investors; for tax return, accrual basis income per CRA rules.

No separate public UBO form is filed for limited partnerships.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: Federal general corporate income tax rate 15% plus British Columbia general corporate income tax rate 12%, producing a combined headline rate of 27% for a taxable corporate partner carrying on business in BC; the BC limited partnership itself is fiscally transparent and has no entity-level corporate income tax liability.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No entity-level income tax for the BC limited partnership. A Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) that is a corporate limited partner may benefit from the federal small business deduction and the BC small business deduction on up to CAD 500,000 of active business income, reducing the combined effective rate to approximately 11%. The UHT oat-milk packaging plant may also generate eligible SR&ED investment tax credits and accelerated capital cost allowance for clean manufacturing equipment. Note: the 5-year loss carryforward figure in this dossier reflects the template convention; under Canadian federal and BC income tax law, unused non-capital losses generally carry forward up to 20 years, with a 3-year carryback.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T5013 Partnership Information Return, T5013 Summary, and T5013 slips; filed electronically through CRA e-File (EFILET5013) or approved tax-filing software and submitted through the CRA's XML/Internet File Transfer system.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Five months after the partnership's fiscal period-end if the partnership has any Canadian-resident partner or a Canadian permanent establishment; eighteen months after fiscal period-end if the partnership has no Canadian-resident partners and no permanent establishment in Canada. The BC filing obligation follows the same deadline because CRA administers the BC Income Tax Act for partnerships.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Partner's share of net business income or loss from the BC UHT oat-milk packaging plant, including plant revenue, raw oat milk concentrate purchases, aseptic packaging costs, depreciation, and operating expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident limited partner must report this allocated amount in a Canadian Part I tax return when the amount is attributable to a Canadian permanent establishment or employment/business activity carried on in Canada; a tax treaty business-profits article may protect the partner if no permanent establishment exists, but the T5013 allocation must still be disclosed to CRA.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Partner's share of other income, including interest, royalty, rental, or foreign-source investment income earned through the partnership.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the income is not attributable to a Canadian permanent establishment and is paid to a non-resident limited partner, Part XIII withholding tax may apply; the partner should provide the payer with Form NR301 and the applicable tax residence certificate to claim treaty reduction.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Partner's share of taxable capital gains from disposition of partnership property, including land, plant, machinery, or packaging equipment.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident partner must obtain a section 116 clearance certificate prior to any disposition if the transaction is reportable; failure to do so can trigger withholding on the gross sale proceeds and additional penalties.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T5013 Summary, Schedule 1, Line 620 / Partnership Identification Area
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total gross revenue, inventory, cost of goods sold, employee wages, sales by jurisdiction, and the principal business activity description corresponding to ISIC 1050 / NAICS 311999.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: The T5013 Summary must be retained with the BC general partner's accounting records and made available to the CRA during audit; non-resident partners should require copies for their own transfer-pricing and treaty documentation.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late-filed or omitted T5013 return: CAD 25 per day, minimum CAD 100, maximum CAD 2,500 under Income Tax Act s.162(3). Knowingly making a false or incomplete return can trigger gross-negligence penalties under s.163(2) equal to 50% of the tax evaded and criminal prosecution under s.239, with fines from 50% to 200% of tax evaded and imprisonment up to five years.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporate Income Tax Return and Schedule 8 (Partnership Income) for any corporate limited partner that carries on business in Canada through the BC limited partnership; filed electronically through CRA e-File or approved tax software.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Six months after the corporation's taxation year-end; quarterly corporate income tax instalments are due, and a corporate limited partner must remit instalments based on its estimated taxable income allocated from the partnership.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net partnership income allocated from the BC limited partnership and reported by the corporate limited partner on its T2 return.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A foreign corporate partner that has no permanent establishment in Canada must not be assessed on business profits under most DTAs; however, it must still file a Canadian T2 return within six months of year-end if it had a Canadian filing obligation or participated in a Canadian-source partnership; a protective T2 should be filed to preserve loss claims and treaty relief.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Small Business Deduction claimed by a Canadian-controlled private corporation on active business income from the partnership.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Not available to a non-resident-owned or foreign-controlled corporation; if the corporate partner is not a CCPC, it must use the federal 15% general rate and BC 12% provincial rate on allocated partnership income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Cross-border controlled transactions with non-residents involving oat-milk concentrate, aseptic packaging materials, intellectual property royalties, management fees, and intercompany debt.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporate limited partner must contemporaneously document arm's-length pricing, file Form T106 if the aggregate value of controlled transactions exceeds CAD 1,000,000, and retain a Master File if the multinational group meets the Country-by-Country reporting threshold of CAD 750,000,000 in consolidated revenue.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late-filed T2 return: 5% of the balance of tax payable plus 1% per month not exceeding 12 months; failure to report a required amount can also attract a separate penalty of 10% of the amount in excess of the correct reporting. Gross-negligence and criminal penalties under ss.163 and 239 apply to intentional misstatement.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% under Part XIII of the Income Tax Act for dividends paid by a Canadian-resident corporation to a non-resident recipient. For a BC limited partnership, a distribution of profit is not a dividend; instead, the non-resident limited partner is taxed under Part I on its allocated share of Canadian-source partnership income. If a Canadian corporate partner distributes such after-tax income as an actual dividend to its foreign shareholder, the 25% statutory dividend withholding rate applies subject to treaty relief.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke treaty relief, the non-resident beneficial owner must complete and deliver CRA Form NR301 (for individuals) or NR302/NR303 (for partnerships/flow-through entities), accompanied by a valid foreign Tax Residence Certificate (TRC) issued by the treaty jurisdiction. The Canadian payer must review the treaty entitlement, confirm the non-resident's status as beneficial owner, apply the OECD MLI Principal Purpose Test, and withhold at the reduced treaty rate before making payment. If the treaty relief is not obtained in advance, the payer must withhold at 25% and the non-resident may claim a refund or reduction through a Canadian income tax return using Form NR7 or by filing an adjusted T1/T2/T5013 position.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: 25% statutory Part XIII rate; treaty-reduced rates commonly 10% for industrial royalties under the Canada-United States DTA and other treaties, with some categories eligible for 0% or 15% depending on the treaty, the type of intellectual property, and the degree of ownership. Interest: 25% statutory Part XIII rate on non-arm's length payments; most arm's-length interest paid at a reasonable rate to a non-resident lender is exempt under Canadian domestic law; treaty rates generally reduce or eliminate withholding on interest, often 0% or 15%, subject to specific DTA language.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1,000,000 in aggregate fair market value of controlled transactions with non-residents in a taxation year, which triggers the mandatory Form T106 information return and contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation. A Local File should also be maintained for the BC UHT plant when the aggregate value of controlled transactions with a non-resident related party exceeds this threshold. A Master File and Country-by-Country Report may be required for multinational groups with consolidated revenue of at least CAD 750,000,000, and CRA may request a Master File for any cross-border related-party transaction even below that threshold when audit risk exists.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not apply Cayman-style Economic Substance Regulations, but the Income Tax Act's general anti-avoidance rule under s.245 and the sham doctrine require commercial substance and a genuine business purpose. The BC limited partnership must have real fixed-place-of-business attributes—an operating UHT plant, physical inventory, employees, plant assets, management decisions, and commercial risk—so that CRA cannot treat it as a conduit, agency, or artificial entity. Treaty benefits can also be denied under the OECD Multilateral Instrument's Principal Purpose Test if obtaining tax treaty advantages was one of the principal purposes of the limited partnership structure.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion and Gross Transfer-Pricing Misstatement
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Submitting false T5013 or T2 records; overstating raw oat-milk concentrate costs through related suppliers; selling finished UHT oat-milk products at a zero margin to a related offshore distributor; fabricating management fees; or maintaining a second set of books for the BC plant.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA may reassess income under s.247 and impose a 10% transfer-pricing penalty on the net adjustment. Gross negligence penalties under s.163(2) add 50% of the tax avoided. Criminal conviction under s.239 of the Income Tax Act is punishable by a fine of 50% to 200% of the tax evaded and imprisonment for up to five years, plus forfeiture and interest compounded daily.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of a corporate general partner who knowingly participate in the misstatement may be jointly and severally assessed for penalties; courts may pierce the corporate veil if the general partner is a mere facade; travel bans, asset freezes, extradition, and imprisonment can be imposed in a criminal tax proceeding, and civil restitution remains a non-dischargeable debt in bankruptcy.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to Withhold and Remit Part XIII Tax
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying royalties, interest, dividends, or management fees to a non-resident related party without applying the 25% statutory withholding rate or using an unsupported treaty position without a valid Tax Residence Certificate; deliberately routing payments through a treaty conduit to skirt Canadian source taxation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The payer is personally liable for the full amount of unwithheld tax under s.215, plus interest and penalty. Negligent non-compliance can lead to a s.227.1 director's liability assessment and a 10% late-withholding penalty plus 20% per year interest; criminal prosecution may result in a fine up to CAD 25,000 per offence and imprisonment for up to 12 months under s.238, or up to five years for tax evasion.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of the corporate general partner are personally liable for withheld taxes not remitted to the CRA, including interest and penalties; the CRA can issue a director's liability assessment without first exhausting the partnership's assets; civil suits and seizure orders may extend to personal bank accounts, residences, and travel restrictions.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Artificial Substance / Treaty Shopping
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating the BC limited partnership as a letter-box entity with no employees, no UHT plant equipment, no substantive executive decisions in British Columbia, and no genuine oat-milk production activity; using the LP merely to originate invoice payments or to claim Canadian treaty benefits for income economically earned elsewhere.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA can recharacterize the arrangement under s.245(2), deny treaty benefits under the OECD MLI Principal Purpose Test, and assess tax, interest, and the 25% GAAR penalty equal to the benefit obtained. The BC limited partner may also lose the limited-liability shield if it participates in control of the business, exposing it to general partner liability for the LP's debts and obligations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and signatories of the corporate general partner may be held personally liable for the partnership's tax debts and civil liabilities if the court finds the entity is an agent or sham; an order can be made to lift the corporate veil, and travel bans can be imposed where evidence of flight risk exists.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML / Financial Crime Red Flags in Trade Settlement
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Executing Swift LC or TT Wire settlements for UHT oat-milk export sales through undisclosed third-party intermediaries; receiving proceeds from shell invoicing companies; failing to verify beneficial owners behind letter-of-credit draws; knowingly processing funds from sanctioned jurisdictions despite the low-risk standard banking tier.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: FINTRAC may issue administrative monetary penalties under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, which can reach CAD 1,500,000 for institutional violations and CAD 500,000 for individuals; criminal money-laundering convictions under the Criminal Code can result in imprisonment up to 10 years, forfeiture of the UHT plant and bank accounts, and debarment from federal procurement.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers who knowingly fail to implement AML/ATF controls, or who direct employees to bypass CDD/beneficial-owner checks, can be charged personally; the court may impose travel bans, seizure of passports, and restraints on disposing of personal and corporate assets, and the Crown may seek civil restitution and punitive damages.
